editorNote: Crew survival, affordable connections and the next generation of home computers fill the desks this week.
morningLine: Fifty missions test a bomber crew; Atari and Commodore promise more; Discovery lifts off.

lead.headline: Fifty missions, one crew: the bomber game that makes survival count
body: Britain is the starting point, but keeping a B-17 and its crew alive is the real destination. Strategic Simulations’ Fifty Mission Crush puts the player in command of an Eighth Air Force bomber for a campaign of fifty missions over Germany, France and the Netherlands. James V. Trunzo’s April COMPUTE! review finds its appeal in sustained command rather than a quick burst of arcade action.

Crew selection gives each mission a personal stake. Fuel and bombs compete for carrying capacity, turning preparation into a consequential decision before the aircraft leaves the ground. The review describes an overloaded bomber crashing on takeoff after an engine failure: extra offensive weight can exact its price immediately.

The campaign has the shape of a role-playing game as much as a flight simulation. Completing one sortie is only a small part of the task; the long sequence of missions gives survival and continuity their weight. Trunzo calls it “a challenging, addictive game.”

At a review-listed $39.95, the disk game serves Atari machines with at least 40K and BASIC, Apple II-series machines with 48K, and the Commodore 64. This is an April review of an available title, not a claim of a debut during this week.
lead.dek: SSI turns the B-17 campaign into a test of preparation, persistence and crew survival.

stories.headline: Atari and Commodore promise a bargain-computer generation
body: April’s COMPUTE! cover report returns to January’s Winter CES and two different answers to the home-computer upgrade question. Atari’s announced 520ST offers 512K, an 8 MHz Motorola 68000 and Digital Research GEM. The proposed $599 computer price and second-quarter availability remain promises, not proof of a machine on a dealer’s shelf.

Commodore’s 128 instead makes continuity a selling point: C64 compatibility, a native 128K personality with BASIC 7.0 and 40/80-column text, and Z80 CP/M capability. These are operating personalities, not three complete independent computers. Tom R. Halfhill tried SpeedScript 3.0 in C64 mode without claiming exhaustive compatibility tests.

Commodore had no formally announced CES price. The report’s under-$300 indication and April-or-May introduction are estimates. For buyers, the decision is between the appeal of a new environment and the value of the programs already at home.

stories.headline: Home-computer optimism meets the PCjr reckoning
body: The Los Angeles Times editorial of April 11 takes the already-announced cancellation of IBM’s PCjr as a warning against easy forecasts. It says IBM was reported to hold more than 100,000 unsold machines; that is the editorial’s attributed estimate, not an audited inventory.

The argument is practical: a household without a specific job such as word processing or financial analysis has less reason to buy. Yet the editorial does not pronounce home computing finished. Its doubts sit alongside new-machine optimism and continuing investment in useful software.

April’s COMPUTE! reviews Lotus 1-2-3 for the Enhanced PCjr at $495. Two ROM cartridges and a floppy bring the spreadsheet to the small IBM, with availability dating from December rather than a new April launch. Hardware retreat and software usefulness can occupy the same desk.

stories.headline: Pooh opens the adventure door without a parser battle
body: Winnie the Pooh in the Hundred Acre Wood gives young players a familiar place to practice observation. Wind has scattered the characters’ possessions; finding objects, identifying their owners and returning them turns the wood into a gentle puzzle.

James V. Trunzo’s April review describes a graphic adventure aimed at seven-year-olds, without the usual typed-command struggle except for directional movement. Owl offers help, a map is available, and object placement changes between games.

The Disney/Sierra title lists at $39.95 in the review. Reading, mapping and logical thinking arrive inside play, while an in-world toybox handles saving without a separate data disk. The review supplies current-month coverage, not a release date for this week.

briefs.headline: Computer Chronicles examines the low end
briefs.summary: Archive catalog dates Low End Computers April 8, 1985; guests Jack and Leonard Tramiel, Frank Leonardi and Gary Kildall; catalog lists Commodore laptop, C128, Amiga and Atari ST demonstrations. Catalog metadata alone does not establish commercial launch dates.

periodAd.headline: A $29.95 connection to the outside world
periodAd.summary: Commodore 1660 Modem 300: April column reports 300-bps direct connection, autodial, autoanswer and monitoring speaker for C64, Plus/4 and C128. Announced price, not a verified local offer.
periodAd.tagline: The modem joins the budget shelf.

market.headline: New promises confront old inventory
market.summary: April 11 editorial skepticism about the PCjr meets Atari and Commodore previews. A promised specification is not stock on a shelf, and a lower announced price does not supply a household with a reason to buy.

worldAnchor.headline: Discovery launches with Senator Garn aboard
worldAnchor.summary: Discovery lifted off April 12 on STS-51D with Senator E. J. Garn among its crew. Communications satellites ANIK C-1 and LEASAT-3 were its payloads.

bbsNote.headline: Cheap modems and faster Delphi put telecomputing within reach
bbsNote.summary: April magazine reporting on January CES links cheaper hardware to wider online access; the travel anecdote illustrates a real non-game use of a laptop modem. These are reported notes, not invented BBS messages.

posts.text: General Videotex announced 2400-bps service in 34 major cities; $5/hour surcharge on ordinary $16 daytime/$6 nonprime rates.

posts.platform: Electronic Official Airlines Guide; service unnamed
posts.text: Levitan recounts using his lap computer, acoustic cups and an information-service local number after a cancelled CES flight, finding five alternatives in about two minutes. Anecdote occurred for January CES, not this April week.
The Learning Phone cartridge was announced for modem-equipped Atari computers, including high-resolution graphics; estimated cartridge price $30–$40, not a verified retail transaction.

curiosity.headline: A home computer offers to analyze your boss
curiosity.summary: Mind Prober turns sixty adjective judgments into a personality report.
curiosity.detail: Richard Mansfield’s April COMPUTE! review describes choosing oneself, a boss or a friend, entering age-category and sex, and agreeing or disagreeing with roughly sixty adjectives. Human Edge charged $29.95 for C64 and $49.95 for other versions. Attribute perceived accuracy to the reviewer, not psychology research.

gadgetWatch.headline: Panasonic combines a speakerphone and modem
gadgetWatch.summary: April column reports KX-D4130 at $199.95: 300-bps modem, hands-free speakerphone, 24-button automatic dialer and storage of up to 30 digits per number. CES-origin reporting, not a proven April launch.
